column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

The entry dates his earldom from about 1136; the article has his appointment by Sigurd I in 1129 and his acclamation as jarl in 1136. Both are given as the article states them; they do not contradict the entry's 'about 1136' for his effective rule, but the editor may wish to check. The entry places his murder in Caithness; the article does not say where, so the place is not given.
Left out: the 2025 and 2026 bills on the Lord High Commissioner and Church appointments, and the long list of later statutory repeals, as detail beyond the entry's scope.
The 1941 campaign's collapse 'within days' is in the entry; the text gives only the mutiny of 10 April and the mobilisation figures.

The entry says she led the Kanhaiya Misl after her husband's death in 1785; the article says she led it from 1789, when her father-in-law Jai Singh Kanhaiya died, and does not date the husband's death. The text gives no year for the start of her leadership. The article dates the arrangement of the daughter's marriage to 1785 and the wedding to 1786; only the wedding year is given.

The entry says Alexander stormed the city of Sangala nearby, which some scholars equate with Sagala; the article identifies the two outright. The text attributes the identification to Arrian's own naming ('a city he calls Sagala and Sangala') rather than asserting it.

Death year: the entry gives d. c. 584. The article's lead says he died in 572; its body says the Annales Cambriae date his death to 584, which may be twelve years too late, giving 572. No death year is given in the text.

The entry says it survived more than 150 years of British rule after 1814; the article gives British control from 1803, formalised by the Treaty of Paris in 1814. The text gives 1803 for full control only, which does not contradict the entry's 1814 for the formal cession.

The article has almost no history beyond Brigham Young's words; the History section is short for that reason. Left out: the Kennecott Land development plan (a forward-looking plan described as recent) and the remark on air quality (a present-day judgement).

Death: the entry gives 1725 at the mission of Jeberos; the article gives 20 March 1725, 1728 or 1730 ('the date is disputed') and says he died in a mission village of the Jivaro Indians. No year is given in the text, and the village is not named.

Left out: the article's confused passages on games, bears and Syracusan feasts, and its contradictory statements on when the votives were deposited. The article says the Romans built a theatre in the 3rd century CE and in another place an amphitheatre; 'theatre' is used, as in the entry.
Death toll: the entry says estimates range up to around 250; the article says at least 250 were killed. No figure for the dead is given in the text.

The entry dates the defeat and execution of Muhammad V to 1577; the article gives no year for the Battle of Webi River and dates the Battle of Addi Qarro to 1577. The text gives neither battle a year. The article dates Hamalmal's revolt to 1563, although he was born in 1550 and elected at about fourteen; the year (and Fasil's 'two years later') is left out as inconsistent.
The article gives his death as 26 May [O.S. 13 May] 1905; the New Style date is used. The suicide is given only as Suzanne Massie's account, since the entry notes murder theories.

The entry dates the creation to 1656–1657 and the residence at Weissenfels from 1680; the article gives 1656 for the duchy and says Neu-Augustusburg was built from about 1660 while Augustus resided at Halle. No year of creation or of the move of the residence is stated in the text.
Living members of the family are not named.

The entry calls it a gift from a king of Baekje; the article's lead and translation say the crown prince of the king of Paekche, while its interpretation section says it is not clear who in Paekche presented it. The text says 'made in Paekche' and gives the crown-prince reading as uncertain. The entry dates it 'usually' to 369; the article discusses 369, 362 and 408. The text gives the traditional reading and Hong's 408 without stating 369, which the entry already gives.

The article gives the proclamation of the republic as 15 December [O.S. 2 December] 1917; the entry uses the Old Style 2 December, so no date for it is given here, and the opening is given in Old Style (21 November; New Style 4 December) so that it does not appear to follow the proclamation. The 1918 dates (18 and 26 January, 6 February) are New Style as the article gives them.
The article spells the capital both Vuga and Vugha; Vuga is used throughout. The article spells the missionary Krapff and Krapf; 'Johann Krapf' is used.

The entry calls him ruler of Lakhnauti who conquered Satgaon and Sonargaon; the article makes him governor (then independent sultan) of Satgaon who conquered Lakhnauti in 1342 and Sonargaon in 1352. The text names the rivals he fought but not their seats, and does not say where his own power began. The 1346 Nepal campaign, which the article ascribes to him 'as the ruler of Satgaon', is given without that phrase. Left out: the article's unsourced claims about an egalitarian administration, and Sanyal's story of his marriage to Phulmati Begum.
Death year: the entry gives 989; the article gives 7 September 988 or 6 September 989. No year of death is stated in the text. Birth: the article gives c. 960, the entry 960; not stated in the text.
The article is short (about 300 words); everything usable is here. It does not give the Ottoman-Safavid chronicle the description mentions, so that is not repeated or expanded.

The article says Liao invaded in 946 and 947 and that Taizong entered Daliang; it gives no exact date for the fall of Kaifeng, so I did not date the surrender. The article gives his death date as 10 July 974 in the lead; I gave only the year, matching the entry.
The article says he was of Tujue extraction; the entry says Sogdian and Turkic descent. Descent left out. The article gives his birth year with a question mark (703?).
The article dates her as queen from about 1773 to 1761 BC; written BCE. Her own seal inscription and the quoted letters left out for length.
Mandela's words are given unquoted in paraphrase close to the article's quotation. The Shosholoza Meyl train and Team Shosholoza left out for length.

The article's line that Sigurd was promised the throne of England and that Harald went to claim it after his death is unexplained and doubtful; left out. The entry's 'last independent king of Ringerike' is not in the article; not repeated.

The article says he 'ruled the Principality of Lippe-Detmold'; the entry calls it a county raised to a principality only in 1789. I avoided naming the territory's rank. The article's census figure is 49416; written 49,416. Short article (about 320 words), so the text is under 300 words.

The article gives the rampart as two miles (3 km) long; the entry says about 4 kilometres. I left the length out. The article names the island Khurte, the entry Kurte; I did not name it. The article spells Siddhis; the entry Siddis. Short article (about 320 words); little more could be said without padding.
The entry speaks of five secondary capitals; the article gives no number, so none is given here. 'Resistance from the capital's aristocrats is likely' follows the article's 'it is safe to assume'.
The article gives 525 BC as the most plausible date, but also cites Whitley for a date after 480 BC. The entry says c. 525 BCE; I said only that the date is debated, without the later figure.

The article dates the mint to the 990s and gives no year for Christ Church's foundation; the entry says around 1030. Neither date given. The article's reign dates are complex (possibly 989-994, 995-1000, restored 1000); I gave none for his accession.

The article says Soba was the capital 'until around 1500'; the entry says it was abandoned after the Funj and Abdallab took it around 1504. I gave no end date. The entry mentions palaces found in excavations; the article says the residence of Alwa's rulers has not yet been identified, so I left that sentence out. The article quotes el-Aswani's 'fine buildings and extensive feelings' (a garbled quotation); I kept only 'fine buildings', unquoted.

The article gives his reign as 1752–1766 and 1768–1784 in the lead, but its text has the Ottomans taking Kutaisi in 1765 and Solomon returning in 1767; the entry says only 'an interruption in the 1760s'. I gave no years for his return. The lead gives his death as 23 April 1784, the text as March 1784; I gave the year only.
Berman's comparison of the Ark with Egyptian portable shrines left out for length.
The entry spells the king Sumanguru Kanté; the article Soumaoro Kante. I used the article's spelling.
The article says the Marshall Islands had not ratified 'as of June 2026'; written only as the signature date. Easter Island, Hawaii and American Samoa lie outside the zone, left out for length.
Hermann Balck's opinion and the Italian spahis of Libya left out for length.
The article spells the minister Pilamathalawe, Pilimatalauwa and Pilimitalava; I used Pilimatalauwa.

The article gives his death as 1678/1681; the entry says 1678. No year given. The article contradicts itself on the chronology of his downfall: it dates the Battle of Virinchipuram to 4 April 1646 but also places it after he was left with only Vellore by 1652, and says Bijapur had conquered Gingee, Tanjavur and Madurai by 1648, while the entry says he had lost his remaining territories by about 1646. I left the battle undated and omitted the 1648 and 1652 dates. It also says Vellore was seized by Golkonda and later that its rule passed to Bijapur; left out.

The article gives the 1771 change as the abolition of the Royal Court's concurrent law-making power; the entry's description already covers it, so not repeated. Present-day officeholders, pay, turnout and the scrutiny panels left out under the present-day rule.

Entry dates c. 1145-1197; the article says she was born before 1153 and died in or slightly before 1190 (by mid-September 1190, when Humphrey was styled lord of Montreal). Birth and death left out. Entry says she married Raynald in 1176; the article says the union was celebrated between late 1176 and June 1177 (lead: 1176 or 1177). No year given for the wedding in the text.
Article is short (about 530 words); the text keeps to it. The article's 'It believed that this local prince was actually Mastigas' is garbled; hedged as 'possibly' and 'some believe'.

Short article (about 330 words); two sections only. The entry speaks of two weeks around the autumn St George's Day; the article gives only the single day, 26 November (Yuri's Day). Both are compatible; the text names the day without the two weeks.
The article spells the heir both Genshin Udugawa and implies the Udagawa family; only 'Genshin' used. Kulmus's book given as originally published in German in 1734 per the article.
SKIPPED: article has about 300 words, nearly all already in the entry's description (parentage, brothers, Pararaton, marriage, successor, Damarwulan legend); only a possible statue is left
The 2021 statue and its controversy left out. Charaideo remained the symbolic centre though the capital moved many times later; not included for length.
The article says the Sulayhids descend from the Hamdanids (via Hashid); left at Hashid since Hamdanids also names the later dynasty.

The article says the manuscript was probably not drafted at Reading but also that the poem was likely composed in Reading (with Leominster as a second possibility); the place of composition is left out.

The article states flatly in one section that he founded the Great Mosque of Demak in 1479, but its lead says other sources credit Sunan Kalijaga; hedged. Some sources make Raden Patah his cousin; left out. Ampel Denta is not in the article.
Zhu Fan Zhi's report of c. 1200 on a Sunda port left out: the article says it probably refers to Banten, not Sunda Kalapa.

The entry dates the massacre of royal relatives to 1879; the article places the succession massacre in 1878 (with 80 to 100 killed). No year and no figure given in the text. Heading 'Career' used rather than 'Reign', since she was queen consort, though historians say she in effect ruled.

The article's speculation identifying the site with Varnu, Bazira or Aornos is left out as unsupported. SK2's 'Era-year 299' reading of Ooemo Takpiso's canal left out as unclear without Harmatta's commentary.
The article spells the general both Görgei and Görgei; the entry uses Görgei. Text uses Görgei as the article mostly does; editor may wish to align with Görgei.

The article names the restorer of 762 as Fujiwara Asakari in the History section and Fujiwara no Nakamaro in the stele section; no name given. The founder is Azumabito Ono in one place and Ono Azumahito in another; the stele form used.
The article says that from 1680 the Ferme Générale bought the right to collect the taille; left out as doubtful (the article's own parenthesis names the aides and gabelle as the farmed taxes).

The article gives his terms as head of state 1928-1931 and prime minister 1928-1932 and 1934-1936; the entry says head of government 1928-1931 and 1934-1936. No end year of the first term and no years for the second given in the text.

The article names the recorder Ilmilku, 'high priest' and 'author' of the three texts; the entry calls him the scribe Ilimilku who copied it. Name and role left out of the text. The daughter is Pugat in the article's opening and Paghat in the narrative; Pugat used.

The article says the Frigideira caused 30 deaths, yet only 34 Portuguese died in the camp in all, and elsewhere says 30 died there between 1937 and 1944; no Frigideira death figure given. Mário Castelhano's listed death date (12 October 1936) precedes the first arrivals; no date given.

The entry dates the split of the realm on Inanch Bilge's death to the 1190s; the article says Tayang succeeded around 1200. No year given. The entry names the battle Chakirmaut; the article calls the clash the Battle of the thirteen sides (probably an error). No battle name given.
The article says the Dutch took the city of Antwerp on 4 August, yet the Dutch already held its citadel and the Belgian Army of the Scheldt surrounded it; left out as doubtful (possibly Turnhout).
The article dates the first Jinchuan campaign 1747–1749, before the entry's span of 1755–1792, and heads the Gurkha campaigns 1788–1793 while its lead gives 1790–1792; neither date range is printed.
The article once calls the Vercelli Book 'eighth-century', a slip against its own tenth-century dating; not used.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance (inventions credited by Pliny, a lost treatise, a bowl in Athenaeus); a longer text would be padding
The oracle of the dead on the Acheron, named in the entry, is not in the article; not mentioned.
The entry's 1633 emigration year is not in the article; no year given for the crossing.

The article says Caesar claims the destruction at the Arar for himself while Appian and Plutarch credit the legate Labienus (Walser judges that more reliable); the entry credits Caesar, so the point is left out. The article treats the Tigurini's Helvetian identity as disputed; the entry states Caesar's view. The text gives the debate as authors' views without saying the entry's statement is wrong.
The article's lead and description date the tomb to about 500-475 BCE, while its finds paragraph and the entry give about 470 BCE; only the lekythos dating is used.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words (course, tributaries, a delta lagoon, a failed defensive line of January 1939) The article gives the river's length as 55 km; the entry says about 60 km.
The article dates Wayne's private council with Little Turtle to 12 August, after the signing on 3 August; the date is left out.
The article says England agreed to suppress piracy (in return for freedom of movement); the entry says both sides agreed to suppress privateering. The text does not say which side undertook it.
The article's lead dates the treaty to 25 September 1379, its Terms section to 9 September 1379 (the entry's date); no day is printed.

The article gives the Slavery Abolition Act as 1833 and emancipation as taking effect on 1 August 1834; the entry says emancipation in 1838. No year is printed. The article dates calypso to 17th-century Trinidad, which sits oddly with the 1780s settlement; not used.
The article gives the party's 2006 result as nine of 289 elected seats in one place and nine of 319 in another; no total is printed.
The article says he became a monk at age 11 and began study in 1065 (he was then 9 or 10); no age is printed. The article gives no years for the stay in China; the entry's 1085-1086 is not repeated.
The article does not name Torda as the place of the 1438 codification; the place is not repeated.

The article dates the one-party state to 1973 (constitution of 25 August 1973); the entry says 1972. No year is printed. The article says Mainza Chona founded and first led the party while Kaunda was imprisoned; the entry says it was led by Kaunda, which holds from 1960.
The 'Leadership' section of the article opens 'As of November 2026'; not used.

The article gives his date as circa 1300 BCE and, citing the Berlin letter, ca. 1340-1300 BCE if the father-in-law was Burna-Buriash II, but adds that some scholars take that Burna-buriash for a later prince and date the reign c. 1275-1240 BCE. The entry has fl. c. 1340 BCE, so the later dating is left out of the text. The article is short (about 270 words); the text keeps close to it. The article writes Ashurbanipal's destruction as 640 BC.
SKIPPED: The article (about 330 words) adds almost nothing to the description, which already covers India, Burma and Siam; only one sentence on the Cambodian Ouparach is new.
The article says Kuwait lost more than two thirds of its territory; the entry says Nejd gained about two-thirds of the land claimed by Kuwait. The share is left out of the text.

The article gives his death as 31 December 1965 (aged 72); the entry's dates are 1893-1966. His death is therefore left out of the text and the last section is headed Legacy. The article's lead says he served under Patel to integrate 562 princely states; the entry says more than five hundred. The figure is left out. The article's Kashmir section gives 25-27 October without a year; the text gives only 26 October after the 1947 date of Junagadh.

SKIPPED: The article has under 200 words on the island itself (area, height, reef, Lomaloma, a sea cave); the rest is a list of notable natives. It also calls the island coral and volcanic where the entry says limestone and volcanic.

The entry calls him one of the successors of Vasudeva I; the article says he followed Kanishka II. The text gives the article's statement without contradicting the entry. Some coins naming Bazodeo have been attributed to Vaskushana; left out.
The article names his teacher both as Kidambi Appullar alias Athreya Ramanujachariar and as his maternal uncle Ātreya Rāmānuja; the text treats them as one person, as the article does.

The entry says the Velay is named after the Gallic Vellavi; the article says there is no explanation of the name except naive 19th-century ones. The text does not discuss the name's origin. The article says the far south-east of the Velay is still the most Protestant area of France; left out as a ranking.

SKIPPED: The article has about 250 words in all, and its main dating contradicts the entry: it says the town was probably laid out in approximately the first half of the second century, where the entry has it laid out after the Boudican revolt of 60-61 (the article dates the revolt to the winter of 61 CE). What is left (the name, the 1928 air photograph, Donald Atkinson's dig, the 2009 Nottingham excavation, the Norfolk Archaeological Trust) is too thin for a longer text.

The article dates his reign 850-871 and puts a war with the Pandyas in 852; the entry has r. c. 848-871 and the capture of Thanjavur around 848. The text gives no year for the capture or the start of the reign. The article says he also defeated the Pallavas; the entry says he ruled at first as a vassal of the Pallavas. The Pallava victory is left out. The article calls him a descendant of Karikala Chola; the entry says he claimed descent from the early Cholas. Left out.

The entry says nothing more is known of his rule. The article's History section credits a 'great prince Višeslav (r. 780-812)' with learning of a Bulgar raid in 783 and says Charlemagne was aided by Višeslav against the Avars, while also saying he is only mentioned by name. Those acts and the reign dates 780-812 are left out; the text keeps to what the article says the DAI records of the Serbs in his time. The entry spells the emperor Porphyrogennetos, the article Porphyrogenitus; the text says only Constantine VII.

The entry names the Banu Kanz under the Fatimids; the article does not mention them, so nothing is said of them here. The article says nothing explicit about New Kingdom mining beyond the stela of Ramesses II.

The entry names Līloa, ʻUmi-a-Līloa and the temple and refuge of Pākaʻalana; the article names only King ʻUmi and the nioi trees of Pakaʻalana (its spelling), so the text says no more about the temple. Left out: the road as the steepest in the world (a ranking) and the 1995 film Waterworld.

Of his wives the article names Alam Ara (Khas Mahal) and Muhammadi Khanum (Begum Hazrat Mahal); only the latter is named in the text. Left out: Bhatnagar's assessment of his character, the Babul Mora thumri and the films.
The article does not mention the Battle of Yehuling, which the entry names; the 1211 campaign is told without it.
The article dates the work 1395-1403; the entry's dates are 1395-1405. No dates are given in the text. Sluter's dates in the article (1340-1405-06) are left out.

The article says it contains 761 pieces and covers the late Warring States to the early Liang; the entry says some 700 works from the Zhou to the Liang. The number of pieces and the starting period are left out. The article dates the compilation to 520-530 / the 520s; the entry has c. 530. No date of compilation is given in the text.
The article calls Renaud 'his brother' and later 'his younger brother'. The entry's quarrel with the abbey of Vézelay is not in the article and is not told here.

The entry gives his governorship as 1741-1749 and 1753-1756; the article says he was recalled as both commander-in-chief and governor in 1757. The year of the recall is left out. The article's text is the lead and section openings only; the Louisbourg section gives no year, so the year of the surrender (1745, in the entry) is not repeated.
The entry names the father Gugong Danfu; the article calls him King Tai of Zhou (the same person). The text uses King Tai and King Ji (Jili) as the article does.

The article gives Rædwald's rule as about 599 to c. 624 but his death as c. 625; the text gives only the start of his reign. Roger of Wendover's dates 571 and 578 are 'respective' to Tytil and Wuffa in the article, which reads oddly (father after son), so the text does not assign them.

The entry dates her campaign against the Song to 1004; the article says she personally led the army against the Song in 1005. The text gives no year for it. The article gives her age at death as 57; with the entry's 953-1009 she would be 55 or 56, so the age is left out.

The article says that at Dafeichuan in 670 Xue inflicted heavy losses before his forces retreated; the entry says he was routed. The text does not describe the battle. The 682 victory over the Eastern Tujue is in the entry and is not repeated.

The article gives his birth as 7 January 1914 (and age 60 at death); the entry dates him 1913-1974, and the article's own titles list starts in 1913. The text gives neither the birth year nor his age at death. The entry says he became Rajpramukh in 1948; the article gives no year, so the PEPSU period is not retold.

The article is a rough translation from Japanese and gives the kingship's span variously (4th to 7th century; 3rd to 7th). The text gives only the researchers' range for its founding, which fits the entry's c. 250. The entry says ties with Baekje brought Buddhism and writing; the article does not say so, and the text does not repeat it.
The article gives his birth as 1545/1546?; the entry has 1545. The text gives no birth year.
The capture of Fu Jiān at Wujiang Mountain and his strangling in 385 are in the entry and are not retold.

The article says Yao Chang fell ill 'around the new year 393' before his death; Yao Chang's own article has him die around the new year 394, and the entry gives Yao Xing's reign from 394. The text gives no date for the accession. The entry says Yao Xing brought Kumarajiva to Chang'an in 401; the article gives 405 for the honorific title only and does not date his arrival. The text gives no year for it.

The article gives his succession as Kapitan both as 1868 and as after Liu's death in 1869; the entry says 1868. The text gives no year for it. The entry calls the conflict the Klang War; the article calls it the Selangor Civil War. Both name the same war; the text uses the article's name.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words, most of it already in the entry

The article gives his reign as 515 until his death in 545, and the pillar inscription as 515-550; it also says he conquered much of India c. 530-540 and that his empire disintegrated c. 530-540. The entry has fl. c. 530. The text gives no reign dates. The stone inscription names Yashodharman and Vishnuvardhana; the article treats them as one ruler in places and two in others. The text keeps the inscription's double name without deciding.
The article places Smbat's capture around 913 and his execution after a year's imprisonment; the entry dates the execution to 914. The text gives no year for it.
The entry says he annexed the Fezzan; the article does not mention it, so the text says nothing of it.

The entry says he took his own life soon after his capture; the article says it is not known for sure whether he was beaten to death or hanged himself in Nanjing. The text says only that he was taken to Nanjing. The killing of Liu Futong in 1363 is in the entry but not in the article.

The article gives his death as 10 April 1969 in the lead and 6 April 1969 in the text; the text gives only April 1969. The entry dates his north-west command from 1946; the article's timeline has him Director of the North-western Headquarters from 1945. The text gives only his Xinjiang governorship, 1946-1947.

The article's account of the Dalai Lama's return and flight is confused (it says Zhao drove him into exile in 1909, then that he fled in February 1910, and mixes quoted passages with other names such as Chao Er-feng). The text gives only the February 1910 flight, which agrees with the entry's 1910 entry into Lhasa. Derge's abolition in 1909, named in the entry, is not in the article.

The article dates his life 175-124 BC and his death to 124 BC; the entry has d. c. 122 BCE. The text gives no year of death or birth. The article says his ministers reminded him that 'his father' kept his distance from the Han, though it calls Zhao Tuo his grandfather; the text says 'his predecessor'.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance, much of it already in the entry
The article gives the founding date as 22 December 1941; the entry has 21 December 1941. The text gives no date. The article does not say the founding units had retreated from Užice.

The article dates the end c. 2900 BC and reports Reisner's view that the culture was destroyed by First Dynasty rulers c. 3100 BC, later revised; I did not restate the end date or cause, which the entry already gives.

Article gives the imamate as about 776 or 778 (lead: 776-777); entry says around 777, so no year was printed. Article's account of 758 and Ibn al-Ash'ath is garbled; entry dates the Abbasid victory to 761. I gave no year for the flight. Death: article 168 AH (784-785 CE); entry d. 784. I printed only the Hijri year.
The article also says Smbat crowned Adarnase king in 899 as a sign of friendship; left out for length.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance, most of it a quotation from Bede; it adds little beyond the entry

The article dates his death between 680 and 685 in the lead but gives the traditional invasion as about 686; the entry says c. 685. I gave no year for the battle. Article dates the absorption of Selsey into Winchester to 686 but Cædwalla's kingship to 687; I left the year of absorption out.

The article gives the collapse of the Chagatai dynasty as 1678; the entry dates Galdan's conquest to 1680. I gave no year. Sources for the Gansu preaching: article says 1671-72 and Xining 1672 (blessing of Qi Jingyi), left out the latter for length.
The article gives no year for the Siege of Multan or Shopian beyond the entry's; the entry has 1818 and 1819 and Peshawar 1834, which the article does not state, so I did not restate them.
The article dates Agaja's use of armoured women against Whydah to 1730 in the history and 1728 in the legacy section; left out.

SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; it also says (citing John Bradley) that the see of Ossory was never at Aghaboe, which contradicts the entry's 'first seat of the diocese of Ossory' and its move to Kilkenny: the entry may need correcting

Death: the article gives 15 December 1897 (and 'died in 1897'); the entry's dates are c. 1836-1898. No year printed. Bandiagara fell 'on April 29th' with no year given (after events of March 1892; the lead says he ruled to 1893); the day was left out.
Curta rejects the Long Life account as a family legend; not included for length.
King David I of Makuria's sack: article 'around 1270', entry 'in the 1270s'; no year printed.
Left out present office-holders, MPs, smuggling detail and the 2001 Ya Basta paragraph (not clearly about Akwesasne).
The entry names al-Basasiri, who does not appear in the article; nothing was said of him.
Birth: the article's lead gives 965 (as the entry) but its lineage section says Rajab 355 AH (June/July 966); no birth date printed.
The article dates his journey to Cairo to 1877 in one section and 1878 in the next; no year printed for it.
Kamatapur: article says he prepared the invasion in 1498 and invaded in 1499; the entry says around 1498. No year printed. Sengupta gives his reign as 1493-1519; entry and article lead 1494-1519.

The article says he died of a heart attack in Bonete en route to Alicante, and later that he died in Cádiz; place of death left out. The article's lead says Algiers badly damaged his reputation; a later section says it did not destroy it. No judgement printed.
The article does not say which Antigonus Thorax was a friend of; left unspecified.
The article gives his life as c. 630 – c. 664 and his kingship 'from 655 until sometime after 664'; the entry has fl. 655–664. Neither birth nor death year is printed.

The article says 'From 1913 to 1915 ... deputy to the Dutch Foreign Office' and also 'He joined the Dutch diplomatic service in 1915'; no year given for entry to the service. The entry's Soetardjo petition is not in the article; not mentioned. Ambassador to France (1946-1948) is in the entry; not repeated.
